lessons.title: Linear Search and Searching Fundamentals
lessons.description: Understand sequential search, invariants, and the trade-offs between ordered and unordered data.
lessons.content:
Searching means locating a target value or determining that it is absent. Linear search checks elements from left to right until it finds a match. It works on unsorted arrays, uses O(1) auxiliary space, and has O(n) worst-case time; its best case is O(1) when the first element matches. If duplicate values exist, returning the first matching index is a useful explicit contract. An empty input returns -1.

Correctness invariant: before checking index i, none of the positions 0 through i-1 contains the target. If the element at i matches, return i; otherwise continue. If the loop ends, every position has been checked and the target is absent.

A hash set or dictionary can offer expected O(1) membership queries after O(n) preprocessing, but costs O(n) additional memory and does not automatically preserve a sorted order. For a one-off search of an unsorted list, linear search is often simpler and sufficient. For many queries, choose a representation based on how often data changes.

lessons.title: Binary Search and Search Boundaries
lessons.description: Search sorted data in logarithmic time and avoid off-by-one errors.
lessons.content:
Binary search requires sorted input (ascending order in this lesson). Maintain an inclusive search interval [left, right]. At each step inspect mid = left + (right-left)//2. If values[mid] equals target, return its index. If it is smaller, discard the left half; otherwise discard the right half. Every iteration shrinks the interval, so the loop terminates in O(log n) time with O(1) extra space.

For duplicate elements, a basic binary search can return any matching index. To find the first occurrence, use a lower-bound search: locate the smallest index i such that values[i] >= target. Maintain a half-open interval [left, right) and return left. Verify that left is in range and values[left] == target. The same approach is useful for insertion positions.

Common errors: binary searching an unsorted list, mixing inclusive and half-open interval rules, forgetting to move boundaries beyond mid, and assuming the first duplicate is returned. In Python, bisect_left implements lower bound for a sorted list.

lessons.title: Bubble Sort, Selection Sort and Insertion Sort
lessons.description: Compare elementary sorting algorithms and their stability and complexity.
lessons.content:
Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps out-of-order pairs. After each full pass, the largest remaining element is in its final position. With an early-stop flag, already sorted input takes O(n) time; worst-case time is O(n²). Adjacent swaps make the usual implementation stable.

Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum of the unsorted suffix and swaps it into place. It performs O(n²) comparisons even for sorted input and at most O(n) swaps. A simple swap-based selection sort is not stable.

Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix: remove the next value, shift larger prefix values one position right, then insert the value. It takes O(n) time on sorted input and O(n²) worst-case time, uses O(1) auxiliary space, and is stable when shifting only strictly greater elements. Insertion sort is especially useful for small or nearly sorted arrays.

For interviews, be ready to trace each algorithm on [5, 2, 4, 1], explain comparisons versus swaps, and discuss why stable sorting matters when records share the same key.

examples.title: Bubble Sort, Selection Sort and Insertion Sort - Python Example
examples.explanation: Run the example with Python 3, then change the inputs and trace each step.
examples.code:
def insertion_sort(values):
    arr = values.copy()
    for i in range(1, len(arr)):
        key = arr[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and arr[j] > key:
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]
            j -= 1
        arr[j + 1] = key
    return arr

print(insertion_sort([5, 2, 4, 1]))  # [1, 2, 4, 5]

lessons.title: Merge Sort and Divide and Conquer
lessons.description: Implement a stable O(n log n) sort by dividing and merging.
lessons.content:
Merge sort divides an array into two halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves. Its recurrence is T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n), yielding O(n log n) time in best, average and worst cases. The straightforward list-based implementation uses O(n) auxiliary memory overall (plus O(log n) recursion stack).

Merging two sorted arrays uses two pointers. Repeatedly take the smaller current item, then append the remaining suffix. Taking from the left half when values are equal preserves the original order of equal-key records; this makes merge sort stable.

The base case is a list of zero or one item. Avoid an infinite recursion by splitting at the midpoint and making both recursive inputs smaller. Merge sort is attractive when predictable performance and stability are important. External merge sort is also useful when a dataset is too large for memory.

lessons.title: Quicksort, Partitioning and Algorithm Selection
lessons.description: Learn pivot partitioning and choose an appropriate searching or sorting strategy.
lessons.content:
Quicksort chooses a pivot, partitions values into elements on either side of the pivot, and recursively sorts the partitions. Partitioning puts the pivot in its final position in common in-place variants. With reasonably balanced partitions, quicksort takes O(n log n) expected time. Repeatedly choosing an extreme pivot can cause O(n²) time and O(n) recursion depth. Randomized pivot selection helps reduce the risk of pathological input.

Typical in-place quicksort implementations are not stable and use O(log n) expected recursion stack space, though worst-case recursion space can reach O(n). By contrast, merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time and can be stable, but usually needs O(n) auxiliary space for arrays.

In production Python, use sorted(values) or values.sort() instead of hand-writing a sorting algorithm unless the exercise explicitly asks for one. Python's Timsort is stable and efficient on partially ordered data. For searching, use linear search on unsorted input, binary search on sorted input, and a set/dictionary for repeated membership lookups when memory permits. State assumptions, test empty arrays and duplicates, and compare time and space before choosing an approach.

quizzes.explanation: Linear search may inspect all n elements.

quizzes.explanation: Binary search discards halves based on sorted order.

quizzes.question: Binary search on n sorted elements has worst-case time complexity:
quizzes.explanation: Each iteration approximately halves the search interval.

quizzes.question: What does lower_bound return in a sorted array?
options: First index with value greater than or equal to target
quizzes.explanation: Lower bound finds the earliest position whose value is at least the target.

quizzes.question: Which sort can run in O(n) time on an already sorted array?
quizzes.explanation: Insertion sort needs one comparison per element on sorted input.

quizzes.question: Which algorithm typically performs O(n²) comparisons even on sorted input?
quizzes.explanation: Selection sort scans the remaining suffix for every position.

quizzes.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
quizzes.explanation: Merge sort splits logarithmically and merges O(n) work per level.

quizzes.question: To make merging stable, which side should be chosen first when keys are equal?
quizzes.explanation: Taking equal keys from the left preserves original relative order.

quizzes.question: What is quicksort’s worst-case time complexity with very unbalanced partitions?
quizzes.explanation: An extreme pivot can leave a subproblem of size n-1 repeatedly.

quizzes.question: Which Python built-in is recommended for general-purpose stable sorting?
quizzes.explanation: sorted() uses Python’s stable built-in sorting implementation.
